title: Filtering and Sorting
summary: Filter rows with WHERE, IN, BETWEEN, LIKE and IS NULL, understand MySQL's case-insensitive comparisons and ENUM ordering, sort with ORDER BY and paginate with LIMIT and OFFSET.
introduction: Reading data is most of what a database does, and almost every read has a WHERE clause, an ORDER BY and often a LIMIT. The syntax is standard SQL, but MySQL adds behaviour you must know: text comparisons ignore case and accents under the default collation, ENUM columns sort by position, LIMIT has a second spelling, and NULL never equals anything. This lesson works through the roastery data one clause at a time and shows the output of every query.
learningObjectives: Filter with comparison operators, AND, OR, IN, BETWEEN and IS NULL
Explain why LIKE and = ignore case under utf8mb4_0900_ai_ci and how to force exact matches
Sort by several columns and paginate with ORDER BY, LIMIT and OFFSET
Format dates and build strings with DATE_FORMAT and CONCAT

blocks.text: `WHERE` keeps the rows for which the condition is true. Comparisons work on numbers, strings and dates alike; `AND` binds more tightly than `OR`, so use parentheses whenever both appear. `IN` is shorthand for a list of `OR` equalities and `BETWEEN` includes both ends.

blocks.code:
SELECT name, roast, price FROM coffees
WHERE roast = 'dark' AND price > 14.50;

blocks.content:
+----------------+----------+
| name           | origin   |
+----------------+----------+
| Decaf Colombia | Colombia |
| Espresso Roast | Brazil   |
| Morning Blend  | Brazil   |
+----------------+----------+
3 rows in set (0.00 sec)

blocks.text: Date and time columns compare as strings in ISO format, so a range of days reads naturally. Remember that `'2025-05-15'` as a `DATETIME` means midnight, which is why the upper bound below spells out the last second of the day; the alternative is `ordered_at < '2025-05-16'`.

`LIKE` matches patterns: `%` stands for any run of characters and `_` for exactly one. Under the default collation `utf8mb4_0900_ai_ci`, both `LIKE` and `=` ignore case *and* accents, so a lower-case, unaccented pattern finds Tomás:

blocks.code: SELECT name FROM customers WHERE name LIKE 'tomas%';

blocks.text: To compare exactly, attach a binary collation to the comparison. Now neither the case nor the accent matches and the result is empty:

blocks.code:
SELECT name FROM customers
WHERE name LIKE 'tomas%' COLLATE utf8mb4_bin;

blocks.title: Case-insensitivity also decides what is a duplicate
blocks.text: Because `=` ignores case, a `UNIQUE` index on `email` treats `Priya@Example.com` and `priya@example.com` as the same value. That is right for emails but wrong for case-sensitive tokens, usernames or file names. Declare such columns with `COLLATE utf8mb4_bin` (or the case-sensitive `utf8mb4_0900_as_cs`) when you create the table, rather than remembering to add `COLLATE` to every query.
For patterns beyond `LIKE`, `REGEXP` accepts regular expressions: `WHERE email REGEXP '^(mei|yusuf)@'`. It is convenient but can never use an index, so keep it for small result sets.

`NULL` means *no value*, and comparing it with `=` yields NULL rather than true, so `WHERE shipped_at = NULL` returns an empty set every time. Use `IS NULL` and `IS NOT NULL`. MySQL also offers the null-safe operator `<=>`, which treats two NULLs as equal, and `IFNULL(shipped_at, 'not yet')` to substitute a value for display.

blocks.code: SELECT id, status FROM orders WHERE shipped_at IS NULL ORDER BY id;

blocks.text: Without `ORDER BY` the row order is whatever was cheapest for the server and may change after an index is added. Sort by as many columns as you need, each with `ASC` (the default) or `DESC`. Watch the `roast` column: it is an `ENUM('light', 'medium', 'dark')`, and ENUMs sort by their position in the definition, not alphabetically.

blocks.code:
SELECT name, roast, price FROM coffees
ORDER BY roast, price DESC;

blocks.content:
+--------------------+--------+-------+
| name               | roast  | price |
+--------------------+--------+-------+
| Yirgacheffe        | light  | 16.00 |
| Decaf Colombia     | medium | 13.75 |
| Morning Blend      | medium | 12.50 |
| Sumatra Mandheling | dark   | 15.25 |
| Espresso Roast     | dark   | 14.00 |
+--------------------+--------+-------+
5 rows in set (0.00 sec)

blocks.text: That positional order is usually what you want for a status column (pending before paid before shipped). To sort an ENUM alphabetically, cast it: `ORDER BY CAST(roast AS CHAR)`. NULLs sort first in ascending order and last in descending order.
`LIMIT` caps the number of rows and only makes sense together with `ORDER BY`; without it the *top three* are three arbitrary rows. `OFFSET` skips rows, which is how pages are built.

blocks.code: SELECT name, price FROM coffees ORDER BY price DESC LIMIT 3;
SELECT id, name FROM coffees ORDER BY id LIMIT 2 OFFSET 2;

blocks.text: MySQL also accepts the short form `LIMIT 2, 2`, where the **offset comes first** and the count second, the reverse of the long form; many pagination bugs come from swapping them. Large offsets are slow because the server still reads and discards every skipped row, so for infinite scrolling prefer *keyset pagination*: `WHERE id > 4 ORDER BY id LIMIT 2`, passing the last id seen.

Any column list may contain expressions, and `AS` names the result. `CONCAT` joins strings (never `||`, as the [introduction](/tutorials/mysql/introduction) showed), and `DATE_FORMAT` renders a date with the same `%` codes you may know from `strftime`.

blocks.code:
SELECT CONCAT(name, ' (', city, ')') AS customer
FROM customers WHERE id <= 2;

SELECT id, DATE_FORMAT(ordered_at, '%d %b %Y') AS placed
FROM orders WHERE ordered_at >= '2025-06-01';

items: Conditions: `IF(stock = 0, 'sold out', 'in stock')` and the standard `CASE WHEN ... THEN ... ELSE ... END`.
`SELECT DISTINCT origin FROM coffees` removes duplicate rows from the result.

blocks.title: Practise the standard parts
blocks.text: Everything in this lesson except the collation behaviour and the short LIMIT form is standard SQL. The [SQL tutorial's WHERE lesson](/tutorials/sql/where) and [sorting lesson](/tutorials/sql/sorting-limiting) let you run similar queries in the browser.

questions.question: Which clause returns the orders that have not shipped?
questions.explanation: NULL is never equal to anything, including NULL, so `= NULL` matches no rows. `IS NULL` is the test for a missing value.

questions.question: How many rows does this return on the coffees table (ids 1 to 5)?
questions.explanation: In the short form the first number is the offset and the second the count: skip 3 rows, return up to 1. Only id 4 is returned.
questions.code: SELECT id FROM coffees ORDER BY id LIMIT 3, 1;
